content: Zinc is a critical trace element essential for the metabolism of proteins, carbohydrates, and lipids. It plays a vital role in neurological development, immune function, and tissue growth. Cells with high turnover rates, such as those in the skin, gastrointestinal tract, immune system, nervous system, and skeletal system of developing infants, require significant amounts of zinc. Zinc deficiency is a global issue, with the World Health Organization (WHO) estimating that 20% of the world's population is zinc deficient. Pregnant and lactating women are particularly vulnerable, with up to 82% potentially having inadequate zinc intake. Serum zinc levels are considered the most reliable biochemical marker of zinc status in populations, and a prevalence of low zinc levels exceeding 20% indicates a significant public health concern. Infants and toddlers are especially susceptible to zinc deficiency due to their rapid growth and high demand for tissue synthesis. Zinc deficiency is more likely in infants who consume human milk combined with plant-based complementary foods low in zinc, particularly in populations where diets are rich in phytates (found in cereals and vegetables), which inhibit zinc absorption. During fetal development, zinc accumulation increases from approximately 240 μg/day at 26 weeks of gestation to 675 μg/day at 36 weeks, averaging 250 μg/kg per day. Preterm and low birth weight infants are at heightened risk of zinc deficiency due to reduced zinc accumulation during the third trimester, insufficient zinc supplementation in parenteral nutrition (PN), intestinal zinc loss from immature or diseased gastrointestinal tracts, increased demand for catch-up growth, and low zinc content in breast milk after initial feeding. Although colostrum contains relatively high levels of zinc, the zinc content in breast milk decreases significantly over time, leading to a negative zinc balance in preterm infants fed human milk. Zinc levels in cord blood and within 96 hours of birth are inversely correlated with gestational age and birth weight. Cord blood zinc levels average 13 ± 3 μmol/L (88 ± 20 μg/dL), while serum zinc levels reach a low point of 9.7 ± 0.7 μmol/L (65 ± 5 μg/dL) at five months of age, which is lower than levels observed in older children and adults. Preterm infants fed human milk often experience a negative zinc balance up to 60 days of life, with zinc levels decreasing further with postnatal age. Zinc levels in preterm infants typically reach their lowest point between six and 12 weeks of age. Clinical signs of zinc deficiency, which may not appear until around three months of age, can be subtle and are often associated with other nutrient deficiencies. Mild to moderate zinc deficiency is characterized by stunted growth, impaired immune function, and compromised gastrointestinal integrity. Zinc deficiency may also be linked to deficits in attention, motor skills, and cognitive development in children, although randomized controlled trials have not conclusively demonstrated that zinc supplementation improves motor or mental development. Subclinical zinc deficiency can result in oxidative stress and a proinflammatory state. Severe zinc deficiency presents with characteristic symptoms such as periorificial and periacral dermatitis, alopecia, and diarrhea. Other associated symptoms include tremors, irritability, jitteriness, hoarse crying, stomatitis, glossitis, paronychia, nail dystrophy, and increased susceptibility to infections. Rare inherited forms of zinc deficiency, such as acrodermatitis enteropathica (caused by reduced intestinal zinc absorption) and transient neonatal zinc deficiency (due to low zinc content in breast milk), are characterized by similar symptoms and are responsive to oral zinc supplementation. Parenteral nutrition (PN) is an intravenous solution used in neonatal intensive care units to meet the nutritional needs of infants who cannot be fed enterally. Preterm infants often require prolonged periods of low enteral intake due to illness, feeding intolerance, or necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC). When PN is necessary, zinc supplementation is typically included to meet the infant's requirements. Preterm infants require higher zinc intake than term infants due to their rapid growth, with recommended intake ranging from 450 μg/kg per day to 500 μg/kg per day to match in utero accretion rates. Standard PN trace element preparations may not provide sufficient zinc, necessitating additional supplementation for preterm infants or those with high zinc losses from diarrhea, stomal output, or severe skin conditions. The European Society of Paediatric Gastroenterology, Hepatology and Nutrition (ESPGHAN) recommends intravenous zinc intake of 250 μg/kg per day for infants under three months of age, 100 μg/kg per day for infants over three months, and 50 μg/kg per day for children, with a maximum daily dose of 5.0 mg. Zinc is the only trace element recommended as an additive to PN solutions for short-term use. Preterm infants, particularly those who are extremely preterm or small for gestational age, face increased risks of mortality, impaired postnatal growth, sepsis, chronic lung disease, NEC, retinopathy of prematurity, and abnormal neurodevelopmental outcomes. Studies have shown that higher nutrient intake is associated with improved postnatal growth and better neurodevelopmental outcomes at 18 months of age in preterm infants. Zinc supplementation may enhance immune function, improve the integrity of the skin and gastrointestinal mucosa, reduce the incidence of nosocomial sepsis and NEC, and improve tolerance to enteral feeding. Additionally, improved epithelial cell repair and postnatal growth may decrease the incidence and severity of chronic lung disease. Enteral feeding with human milk alone is insufficient to maintain a normal zinc balance in preterm infants. Recommended enteral zinc intake for preterm infants ranges from 1.1 mg/kg per day to 2.0 mg/kg per day, with the zinc-to-copper molar ratio in infant formula not exceeding 20. Supplementing PN with zinc can address this deficit and prevent clinical and biochemical zinc deficiency. Cochrane Reviews have evaluated the efficacy of zinc supplementation in various populations. Zinc supplementation in pregnant women in low-income settings has been shown to reduce preterm births, although it does not significantly affect the incidence of low birth weight. In infants and children, zinc supplementation reduces the incidence and prevalence of pneumonia, a leading cause of death in children. Zinc supplementation also shortens the duration of diarrhea and persistent diarrhea in areas with high zinc deficiency prevalence, although this effect has not been observed in infants under six months of age. These findings suggest that zinc supplementation may play a role in reducing susceptibility to and severity of infections in newborns. Zinc deficiency is a widespread issue, with an estimated 20% of the global population affected. WHO estimates that approximately 800,000 deaths annually are related to zinc deficiency, with over half of these deaths occurring in infants and children under five years of age. Low birth weight infants, including those born preterm or small for gestational age, are at particularly high risk of zinc deficiency. Zinc supplementation has demonstrated benefits in specific populations, such as reducing preterm delivery in pregnant women and preventing pneumonia and shortening diarrhea duration in infants and children. Supplementing PN with zinc has the potential to prevent zinc deficiency and improve outcomes for low birth weight and critically ill newborns.
